newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia can manage without IMF credits - Davydov.
newsitem.headline: Russia can manage without IMF credits - Davydov.

text.p: Russia can do without the International Monetary Fund's money if the IMF insists on too rigid an application of economic reforms, Minister for Foreign Economic Relations Oleg Davydov was quoted as saying on Monday.

"The tranches of the extended credit, which are withheld from time to time by the IMF on different pretexts, mean just nothing to us," Interfax news agency quoted Davydov as saying in an interview. "The Russian economy is stabilising and is perfectly well able to do without this money."
A spokeswoman for Davydov confirmed the text of the interview, and said he had given it on Friday. It was not clear whether his comments represented government policy.
The government on Monday issued a resolution naming Finance Minister Alexander Livshits head of the government commission on foreign debt and financial assets in place of Davydov.

Davydov, who is also a deputy prime minister, had negotiated Russia's rescheduling agreements with the London Club of commercial bank creditors and Paris Club of official creditors, but was not usually involved directly in talks with the IMF.
"The advice of the IMF on Russian economic reform is solely in the nature of a recommendation from Moscow's point of view. We listen to it but take the decisions ourselves," he said.
"The IMF does not have an absolute monopoly on truth."
Davydov said the IMF was using a tough approach to Russian reforms worked out by Harvard University economists.
"This scheme, largely orientated towards the macro-economic level, is far from being suitable for Moscow," he said.

The IMF has delayed a decision on paying out the latest $330 million of its $10 billion three-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF) for Russia, mainly because it is worried by Russia's poor tax collection performance.
A Fund mission is currently in Moscow reviewing the economy and looking in particular at taxes, before deciding whether to recommend paying out the tranche or not.

Last week First Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Ilyushin, who is in charge of social policy, said Russia, which is behind in paying pensions, may have to risk offending international monetary organisations in order to pay pensioners.
